title: Révisé Cardiac risque index pour Pre-Operative risque
abbreviations: Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk
formula:
Addition des points sélectionnés :

| Facteur de risque | Description | Points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chirurgie à haut risque | Intraperitonéale ; intrathoracique ; vasculaire sus-inguinale | +1 |
| Antécédent de coronaropathie | Antécédent d'infarctus du myocarde (IM) ; antécédent d'épreuve d'effort positive ; douleur thoracique actuelle attribuée à une ischémie myocardique ; traitement par dérivés nitrés ou ECG avec ondes Q pathologiques | +1 |
| Antécédent d'insuffisance cardiaque congestive | Œdème pulmonaire, râles bilatéraux ou galop B3 ; dyspnée paroxystique nocturne ; radiographie thoracique (CXR) montrant une redistribution vasculaire pulmonaire | +1 |
| Antécédent de maladie cérébrovasculaire | Accident ischémique transitoire (AIT) ou accident vasculaire cérébral (AVC) antérieur | +1 |
| Traitement préopératoire par insuline | -- | +1 |
| Créatinine préopératoire >2 mg/dL / 176,8 µmol/L | -- | +1 |

how_to_use.why:
- Fournit une stratification du risque individualisée avant la chirurgie, ce qui peut être utile dans les discussions de consentement éclairé.
- Comprend 6 variables objectives et binaires, avec un score additif.
- Chez les patients à risque élevé (RCRI ≥1, âge ≥65 ans, ou âge de 45-64 ans avec une maladie cardiovasculaire significative), cet outil oriente la stratification du risque préopératoire supplémentaire (p. ex., NT-proBNP ou BNP sériques) et détermine la surveillance cardiaque postopératoire appropriée (p. ex., ECG, troponines).
how_to_use.when:
- Patients ≥45 ans (ou 18-44 ans avec une maladie cardiovasculaire significative) devant subir une chirurgie non cardiaque programmée ou une chirurgie non cardiaque urgente/semi-urgente (non émergente).
- À utiliser avec prudence chez les patients subissant une chirurgie d'urgence ou une chirurgie vasculaire, car le score est moins bien validé pour la première et sa performance est connue comme étant médiocre pour la seconde.
how_to_use.pearls:
- Facile à utiliser par toutes les spécialités concernées, notamment la médecine interne générale, la cardiologie, l'anesthésie et la chirurgie.
- Peut être utilisé en contexte préopératoire hospitalier ou ambulatoire.
- Inclut un nombre limité de facteurs de risque, en partie parce que les études originales n'incluaient pas un nombre suffisant de patients pour chaque facteur de risque important (p. ex., il sous-estime les résultats hémodynamiques et cardiovasculaires dans les valvulopathies).
- D'autres résultats importants pour les patients non évalués par cet outil incluent le risque d'accident vasculaire cérébral, d'hémorragie majeure, d'hospitalisation prolongée et d'admission en soins intensifs.
- Bien que la [Société canadienne de cardiologie 2017](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27865641) ait spécifié le RCRI dans son algorithme d'évaluation cardiovasculaire préopératoire pour les patients subissant une chirurgie programmée, des recommandations plus récentes [européennes (2022)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36017553/) et [américaines (2024)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39320289/) ne recommandent plus aucun outil spécifique.

next_steps.advice:
According to the[2017 CCS Perioperative Guidelines](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27865641):

- If the RCRI is ≥1, the patient’s age is ≥65, or they are between 45-64 years old with significant cardiac disease, consider obtaining NT-proBNP or BNP.
- If the NT-proBNP is ≥300 ng/L or BNP is ≥92 ng/L, then an EKG should be ordered in the PACU, and troponins should be measured daily for 48-72 hours.
- If, after risk stratification, the NT-proBNP is <300 ng/L or BNP <92 ng/L, no routine postoperative cardiac monitoring is recommended.
- If these assays are not available, then patients should be monitored with an EKG in the PACU and troponin measurements daily for 48-72 hours if they meet any one of the following additional criteria: known history of coronary artery disease, cerebral vascular disease, peripheral artery disease, heart failure, severe pulmonary hypertension, or a severe obstructive intracardiac abnormality (e.g., severe aortic stenosis, severe mitral stenosis, or severe hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy).

The data supporting the use of NT-proBNP/BNP comes from a large 2014 meta-analysis of 18 studies with a total of 2,477 patients ([Rodseth 2014](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24076282)). This study, which was in agreement with multiple previous meta-analyses, noted that for patients with a pre-operative NT-proBNP of <300 ng/L or BNP <92 ng/L, the rate of 30-day postoperative non-fatal MI or death was 4.9% (3.9%-61%), and was 21.8% (19.0%-24.8%) in those with pre-operative NT-proBNP is ≥300 ng/L or BNP is ≥92 ng/L.

evidence:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI; also called the Lee index) is an update to the older, 9-item risk score by Goldman et al., published in 1977.[Published in 1999](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10477528/), the RCRI was a 6-item risk score derived and validated for predicting myocardial infarction, pulmonary edema, ventricular fibrillation or primary cardiac arrest, and complete heart block in 4,315 patients aged 50 or above who underwent nonemergent, noncardiac procedures with an expected length of stay ≥2 days at Brigham and Women’s Hospital between 1989 and 1994. The original study used the hold-out method, where two thirds of the patients (i.e., n=2,893) were used for deriving the model, and one-third (i.e., n=1,422) was used for validating the model. Here, the RCRI achieved an AUROC of 0.759 in the derivation cohort and 0.806 in the validation cohort.

Of note, the model was derived using a two-stage process using logistic regression, with the first stage involving univariable regression to screen for potential predictors, which were then included in the second stage that further selected significant predictors using stepwise logistic regression. Such an approach has since been found to be of questionable reliability and has been largely superseded by other variable selection methods such as LASSO and elastic net regression. Initially, generalizability of the model was limited for a variety of reasons. Death was not part of the outcome, and the use of logistic regression implied that competing risks were not taken into consideration, which may have been partially mitigated by the short outcome duration. The derivation study also excluded patients expected to require <2 days of hospitalization, and the authors observed that those who did not consent to the study had significantly higher rates of postoperative cardiac events (1.7% versus 4.8%; P<0.001).

Since the publication of the[original study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10477528/)in 1999, a large number of validation studies have been performed. These were summarized in a systematic review by[Ford et al., in 2010](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20048269/), which found that the RCRI had moderate discrimination ability for cardiac events after mixed non-cardiac surgery (AUROC 0.75 [95% CI, 0.72 to 0.79]). However, an important caveat was that most studies included in this systematic review did not study the same outcome as the original study by Lee et al. In fact, of the 24 meta-analyzed studies, only 1 (aside from the original study) used the same outcomes. In studies that included death as part of the outcome, the AUROC values were substantially lower (0.62 [range, 0.54 to 0.78]).[A subsequent study by Cohn and Ros](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29126584/)confirmed that the RCRI had good discriminatory ability for postoperative cardiovascular events as defined by the original study but was not significantly predictive of 30-day mortality. A more contemporary study by[Roshanov et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33766613/)found the RCRI to have mediocre discriminatory ability, with an AUROC of only 0.69 [95% CI: 0.65-0.72]. This raises the possibility of issues with the model’s temporal validity, i.e., whether over-time changes in care and patient characteristics have substantially impacted its performance.

Other studies have claimed that the RCRI severely underestimated the risk of cardiac events. This was partly true, likely due to the increasing use of troponin measurements for diagnosing myocardial infarction since the publication of the original study. However, many such studies also looked at outcomes that differed substantially from what was used in the original study, which may have also contributed to apparent underestimation.

The omission of cardiac death meant that the outcome deviated significantly from the conventional definitions of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), which has become a common endpoint for other similar risk scores. To this end, and to address concerns with calibration, the[2017 Canadian guidelines](http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27865641)have pooled estimates from several high-quality validation studies to update the estimated risk for each score level, with the outcome changed to include 30-day mortality. These estimates were also reported by the[2022 European guidelines](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36017553/).

However, it is worth noting that only one of these studies, the[VISION Pilot study](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22567075), had the goal of prospectively validating the RCRI; all other studies ([Rajagopalan et al.](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18586440),[Ausset et al.](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17666156), and[Sheth et al.](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25902738)) did not aim to do so specifically but reported appropriate and poolable estimates. Another large international prospective study by[Roshanov et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33766613/), which was a secondary analysis of the VISION study, was published in 2021. It should be pointed out that the latest[2024 American guidelines](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39320289/)do not list the exact risk estimates for each score level, and instead refer to an RCRI >1 as denoting elevated risk.

Lastly, it is worth mentioning that the RCRI is known to perform poorly in patients undergoing vascular surgery, possibly because the indications for such procedures typically carry a higher cardiac risk. In particular,[a 2019 study by Fronczek et al.,](https://www.bjanaesthesia.org/article/S0007-0912(19)30433-7/fulltext)using data from the VISION study, showed that both the RCRI and the NSQIP MICA risk score underestimated the risk of major cardiac events in patients undergoing vascular surgery, with both showing no clinical utility at all in decision curve analysis.
more_info:
Interprétation selon l'étude originale de 1999. Les valeurs sont basées sur une combinaison des cohortes de dérivation et de validation.

| Score RCRI | Risque approximatif d'événement cardiaque majeur (IC 95 %)* |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | 0,5 % |
| 1 | 1,1 % |
| 2 | 5 % |
| ≥3 | 10 % |

*Les [recommandations américaines de 2024](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39320289/) ne listent pas les estimations exactes de risque pour chaque niveau de score et se réfèrent plutôt à un RCRI >1 comme indicateur d'un risque élevé.

**Les recommandations CCS de 2017 et ESC de 2022 proposent des niveaux de risque alternatifs basés sur le score RCRI. Envisager d'ajuster l'interprétation selon la région.

medium_description: Estime le risque de complications cardiaques après une chirurgie non cardiaque.
